newsitem.title: USA: U.S. health insurers moving quickly to merge.
newsitem.headline: U.S. health insurers moving quickly to merge.

text.p: U.S. health insurers are moving quickly to seal deals to gain the national presence and crucial market share needed to survive as customers abandon traditional indemnity plans in favor of managed care.
And the pace is likely to quicken as each deal puts renewed pressure on competitors to take action, analysts and bankers said.
"It's an industry in transition. Everybody's talking to everybody. I think you're going to see continued consolidation among the various companies," an investment banker said.
"It sort of comes in waves. Every action ends up with another reaction," he added.
"When one of your major competitors is now twice your size because of a pending merger, it prompts you into action just to be competitive."

In just the last two months, the industry has seen several major deals announced. In August, California-based PacifiCare Health Systems Inc agreed to acquire FHP International Corp, also in California, in a deal valued at about $2.1 billion.
That pushed two other California-based companies, Foundation Health Corp and Health Systems International Inc, into a merger announced this week valued at about $3 billion.

Also this week, Blue Cross & Blue Shield of Connecticut agreed to a merger with Indianapolis-based Anthem Inc, and last week Empire Blue Cross and Blue Shield said it would seek to convert itself into a for-profit organization to meet the increasing competition in the healthcare industry.
And more deals are expected.

Speculation of a deal between California-based WellPoint Health Networks Inc and Massachusetts-based John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co intensified this week following newspaper reports that they were in talks.
Both parties have declined to comment.
Wellpoint earlier in the year acquired the life and health benefits management division of Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Co.
"When your competitors are getting to be significantly larger than yourself, it makes sense to go out and buy somebody so you can keep up," said Sanford C. Bernstein analyst Clifford Hewitt.
And companies such as WellPoint and Anthem are expected to continue to be active acquirors as they seek to expand beyond their regional strongholds.
"I see a very clear pattern of consolidation by a handful of organizations that want to create a national presence in managed care," another banker said.
He and others said they expect the managed care industry to consolidate down to just 15 or 20 major companies.
The rapid consolidation comes as local and regional managed care companies scramble to patch together the market once dominated by the traditional indemnity plans.
Those smaller managed care companies have needed to build market share and expand into new markets to be more efficient and cost effective.

"You're still in a period in which HMOs need to grow market share and create strong presence in a variety of regions around the country and the easiest way to do that is through acquisitions," Hewitt said.
And as major corporate clients abandoned indemnity plans for managed care, it has forced the traditional health insurers to expand into managed care or exit the health business entirely.
Travelers, for instance, exited the health insurance business last year when it sold its 48 percent stake in MetraHealth Cos Inc to United Healthcare Corp.
Managed care companies also have sought out the indemnity business of rival health insurers in the hopes of converting them to managed care at a later date.
That appears to be part of the strategy behind Wellpoint's interest in Hancock's indemnity business.
"You're buying an existing customer base, client relationships," Hewitt said. Such a move also would give Wellpoint a greater presence on the East Coast.
But, the indemnity business offers buyers little hope of growth, analysts said.
"On the indemnity side, ultimately it's going to disappear," Hewitt said. "It's just a question of time."
